utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber informs the parties that for a series of reasons we'll not sit on Thursday, and I do understand that this accommodates some of Defence counsel, especially that -- it's for your information. Then Mr. Waespi, before we start, you do remember that the Chamber wished not to be overloaded by exhibits, so therefore, I don't know what you had in your mind, but, of course, the guidance of the Chamber was only to tender to those documents that were referred to in the examination-in-chief. But this is not to say that not -- perhaps a very short list of documents to which reference was made can be tendered from the bar table. But that really should be extremely limited, if what is clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President. In fact, I will be focusing on tendering a few remaining documents, I think about 12, and perhaps if there's a balance of a few more, I would tender them by bar table, but I will see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Theunens, I want to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's conclude the topic notice with four documents. The first one is 65 ter 1998. And this is a document, a daily report, up to 1900 hours, dated 6th of August, by Colonel Ivan Zelic. First of all, can you tell us who Ivan Zelic is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Colonel Ivan Zelic is the assistant commander for political affairs of political matters in the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to English page 3, and I think it is the second page in B/C/S. And I quote from the middle of the page: "The entry itself of our members and the treatment of civilians was proper and at the required level. However, the behaviour of our members regarding property found was catastrophic. Immediately after entry the devastation of buildings and uncontrolled collection of war booty began, but VP units had already entered the town and manned the main check-points preventing further destruction and devastation of property." What's the significance of this document, in terms of notice, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, like any other document we have seen so far should not be considered in isolation, and before answering the question, I would like to come back to my testimony of Friday when I was questioned in court about possible reasons for General Tolj to issue an instruction on, was it on the 1st or 2nd of August, 1995, during or after Ljeto, that the church in Glamoc should not be burned. I presented what I described in my testimony as a quite likely option during my testimony, obviously, I had not analysed or commented on Tolj's instruction in the war diary or the operation diary in my report because it was just an isolated information. Analysis not about trying to draw conclusions from one line or two-line entries in the document, but it is about distinguishing or identifying patterns and trends. And in light of that, on Friday, it was concluded that my comment or the -- what I described as the quite likely option was outside of my field of expertise or maybe even lacking neutrality. I think that is a serious issue. Because as a professional intelligence analyst, one of the things you learn to be careful with biased, and we are biased. We are biased by the area the part of the world where we are born, the education we are undergo, the people we meet, the people who influence us. The most important to Be aware of that and to try to take measures against it. And intelligence analysts are trained in that, at least the analysts I know. One of the basic works in that area is the Phycology Of Intelligence Analysis by Richard J. Hoyer. To come back to this question, the document cannot be considered in isolation. We have here the assistant commander for political affairs who informs his superior along the professional line, General Tolj, about the situation in Knin on the 6th of August. We know from the entries in the war diary and other information which is discussed on page 127 in my report, that it are the 4rd and 7th Guards Brigade who enter anyone in the course of the morning of the 5th of August and then seize control over the entire city. The report by the assistant commander for political affairs is useful, but it's not only the only source of information for the operational commander to know what is happening. We know that he has to be aware of the situation. He would have been informed also through other channels. For example, the military police as well as the commanders of the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigade when they inform the commander about the degree of implementation of the orders he has received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just object, note an objection to the forms of the question. I think given the answer, the open ended question about what is the significance of this tends to invite the witness to give rather long answers and to some extent a speech at the beginning. And if we could focus the questioning to get a focussed answer from the witness, that would be my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That is a perfectly proper way to ask an expert about a document. I think the witness, in this specific incident, wanted to get back to a comment he made on Friday. That is the issue about the perhaps length of this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, if there is any reason to go back to what he testified earlier, then would you please guide him. And, first of all, the question was whether -- what the relevance was, what the significance, but it was specified as far as notice is concerned. Mr. Waespi, to the extent possible, please be focussed in your questions, and there's some merit in Mr. Misetic says, although not such a level that I am stopping you, but I invite you to put questions as much possible focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1132 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to next document, which is 65 ter 2304. Now, this is a document dated 10th of August, 1995, and it is an overall report on the security situation in the zone of responsibility of OG north, and it comes from the assistant commander for SIS, OG north, Zeljko Pavic. Now we have seen this author before. Can you tell us again who he is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Zeljko Pavic, as we can see on page 10 of the report is the assistant commander for SIS, which stands for security an information in OG north, and OG north is one of the four OGs that still existed at the time of the report within Split Military District. The main units ever OG north are the 4th Guards Brigade and the 7th Guards Brigade. There are other units included, and these can be found on English page 101, as well as 106 in my report, second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let go to English page 7, B/C/S page 3. The English at the top of the page. And I quote: "As HV members entered the town of Knin, some of them did not act in a civilized manner. They were demolishing shops and running tanks over cars." And the next quote is on page 9 in English: "In keeping with an order of the Split ZP commander -- Colonel General Ante Gotovina. Military police officers are to regroup their forces and assign enough members to secure all of the aforementioned depots." Now, does that confirm or not what you told us or not on Friday about the subordination of the military police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, we see that -- this is discussed in my report, English part 2. English pages 206 to 223. I discussed the use of military police by the Split Military District during and after Operation Storm. And from the documents I have reviewed there, one can conclude that prior to the 9th of August, military police are mainly used for combat tasks, and in the regular -- for the regular military police tasks, they are subordinated to the operational commander. The Military District Commander General Gotovina or the Operational Group Commander. And then after the 9th of August, 9th, 10th of August, we see that military police forces of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalion are increasingly used for what I would describe as traditional military police tasks, i.e., tasks that are also included in Article 10 of the 1994 military police rules which is here P880. And, yeah, this entry, it states what is it states. It is General Gotovina who can issue orders on the regular tasks of the military police. I would also like to draw your attention to an entry that was not addressed by Mr. Waespi, and this is an entry on English page 4. This is an overall report, not just a 24-hour report covering 24 hours, but it covers actually the conduct and the developments during Operation Storm as well as the aftermath of Operation Storm. And if we go to English page 4, there is a title, 3, Relations And Problems With UNCRO, and the author of the report there states -- and I'm reading from the report: "In the course of the operation, 11 foreign journalists who tried to enter the zone of operations of OG north were sent back from military police check-points in a number of locations." And that I believe is important in light of my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be page 2 or 3 in the English, rather than page 4, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, okay, we're on the right side of my monitor, I see the first page with the first title. Then the next page should be summary of the operation coordination with SIS officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What it should be, I -- here we have relations and problems with UNCRO which, for me, appears on page 2 at the bottom. Just for those who will consult the record at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will correct that. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I need make a correction to the record. The last exhibit, which was 65 ter 01998, should have been Exhibit P1133. The current exhibit, 65 ter 02304, becomes Exhibit P1134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is now put on the record what P1133 is, and that was already admitted into evidence. P1134 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to move to 65 ter 5796. And, first of all, I'd like to orally move this document on to the 65 ter list, because it's not yet there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. -- I think the guidance was that if there were any objections -- if there are no objections against admission, this is understood to no objections against adding it to the 65 ter list. So we do not deal with it, with this witness at least, separately. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 9th of August, 1995 from Colonel Mirko Klavic to Colonel General Ante Gotovina. And it is talks in the first paragraph about "the area of responsibility of the 142nd Home Guard Regiment that there were incursions into their zone by military and civilian individuals from the direction of Drnis. This was followed by raids on houses, torching, destruction, and the taking away of combat hardware and other material means which, objectively, from their positions, our soldiers were not able to and were not in a position to stop. Similar occurrences, without the torching, took place in the course of 7 and 8 August also." Now, does that confirm or not what you told us earlier about notice to the commander of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours, and I would like to add that we are confronted with a particular problem here because these locations: Miocic, Biocic, Kricke are small hamlets, which are located just east of the Drnis-Knin road, and based on my understanding of deployment maps and the zone of responsibility, this is on the limit between the zone of responsibility of OG Sibenik, or Operation Group Sibenik, I apologise. The 142nd Home Guard Regiment belongs to OG Sibenik which is located on the western side, and then we have OG Sinj which is located on the eastern side, whereby the 6th Home Guard Regiment belongs to OG Sinj. So the commander of the 6th Home Guard Regiment complains with the his superior, the commander of the Split Military District, about a problem that he notices in his zone of responsibility which is created by members of a neighbouring unit. So the limits between zones of responsibility can be problematic in the military, in particular if they're not clearly visible, and this is not only during the conduct of operations but also afterwards, i.e., when consolidating control over a particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, before you continue you say that he is complaining about problems created by members of a neighbouring unit. Isn't he dealing with military and civilian individuals? Because before you continue, what you are telling us now is that a purely -- a matter of military from other units interfering, or is it a matter ever military and civilian individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. It is a matter of military and civilians. However, again, based on the other documents I have reviewed and also based on doctrine, a military commander is responsible for his zone of responsibility. When we discussed the plan of security, on Friday, there were instructions given on the control of the access of civilians. It is my understanding of military doctrine as well as the other documents I reviewed, that certainly at that early stage, the military commander is in charge, and he has to use his assets, his troop, military police. If there is civilian police, he has to coordinate with them in order to prevent people who are not authorized to be present in his zone of responsibility from preventing to enter his zone of responsibility. Because the civilians can be anyone. They can indeed be displaced persons who want to go back to their house. They can be people coming from somewhere elsewhere else with criminal motives. They can also be members of the enemy forces who have stayed behind and want to create problems. So what I am trying to is that the military commander has all interest in establishing the highest degree possible of control in his zone of responsibility. The fact that the commander of the 6th Home Guard Regiment addresses his concern to General Gotovina indicates that he expected is General Gotovina is someone who can assist him in solving the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do you find this indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document, this report, is based on the address list only directed to the commander of the Split Military District, Colonel General Ante Gotovina, as we see on the front page, top right corner on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But is there any clear expectation, please assist me in this or that way, or is he just reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the military reporting is done with a particular goal. That's why there are templates for reports, and that's why also instructions are given as to what has to be reported. If the commander of the 6th Home Guard Regiment reports his information to General Gotovina, he does it with a particular purpose. Otherwise I assume there would be many other topics he could contact General Gotovina about. The commander of the 6th Home Guard Regiment knows that is he responsible to General Gotovina for the situation in his zone of responsibility. That is something we can derive from doctrine, as well as earlier documents or orders we have seen where the superior commander in the last paragraph of the order usually states that he holds the addressee of the order responsible for the implementation of the order. So the commander of the 6th Home Guard Regiment knows that Gotovina, excuse me, General Gotovina will hold him responsible for the situation in his zone of responsibility. The commander of the 6th Home Guard Regiment feels, or has the opinion, that he is not able to maintain order in his zone of responsibility because of problems created actually by what he describes as military and civilian arriving from the zone of responsibility of the 142nd Home Guard Regiment. So at least from the military point of view, it is logical that he seeks assistance through a report from his superior commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or he reports that he has done everything he could and that he failed to keep matters under control. I do not see anywhere that he says, Please assist me or -- you say that is all implied and that's logic, rather than ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we go to part 1 of the report, I have a section on the planning and the conduct of commander operations. We have discussed the importance of situational awareness, that a commander has no know what is happening in his zone of responsibility. It is not just an exchange of knowledge. The information that is being exchanged has to serve a purpose because command and control is a process, which means that there is a continuous flow of orders, and in order to -- to issue those orders well, there has to be information, situation on the situation in the area, relevant information that will be on enemy situation, friendly situation, the terrain, and all other aspects that are relevant in view of the eyes of the military commander in order to be able to do his -- his job as a military commander. It is clear and it is correct that the commander of the 6th Home Guard Regiment does not ask General Gotovina explicitly to do something, but at least from the military point of view, it doesn't make sense to just report something without anybody acting upon that report or upon that information. The military information that is being shared has to serve a purpose. That's why it's shared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P1135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1135 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last document I'd like to discuss in this section is 65 ter 3461.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is a document dated 23rd August 1995. Subject, operative group north, evening briefing and intelligence data. And it's authored by leader Zoran Lasic. And the specific entry I'd like to refer you to is on page 2 in the English. In the middle, "... propaganda, the problem of looting, and arson on the territory of municipality of Glamoc and Grahovo is present again. Such behaviour causes a great damage to the Croatian people and to the promotion of our state in the world. The problem: Discipline an organisation." Now first of all who is Zoran Lasic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Lasic is the leader of the SIS in the operative team or the OG north. On the 18th of August, and that is discussed in part 2 of the English version of my report. On the 18th August, General Gotovina issues an order to rename the operation groups in the Split Military District. We have then an OG JUG.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I think for the sake of clarity, if Mr. Theunens could specify whether this is SIS of the Split Military District or the SIS of the HVO. I think it could be important for the Chamber to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could include an answer to that question in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. So General Gotovina on the 18th of August, issues an order to rename the existing OGs. This order can be find on 65 ter 3361. The previously existing OG Sajkovic becomes OG JUG, south. OG Otric becomes OG Zapad, west, and OG Vrbanja becomes OG north. Brigadier Zeljko Glasnovic [phoen] is a general or an officer of the HVO. However, OG north as well as all elements of OG north including the SIS section of OG north, at that time are subordinated to General Gotovina. As we can see from the document OG north consists of a number of tactical groups which is in line with the doctrine, and in relation to the entry on page -- English page 2, the reference -- the use of the word "again," based on the other documents I reviewed in the preparation of my report, refers to the events that occurred in Grahovo and Glamoc during and after operation Ljeto, i.e., between 28 of July and early August. And here we see that this HVO general expresses his concern about what he describes as the great damage to the Croatian people and the promotion of our state in the world. And I quote: "The problem of looting and arson on the territory of Glamoc and Grahovo threatens to create."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do then understand that is the -- SIS is an element in the HVO, but subordinated to Operational Group north. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. In relation it to this particular SIS cell because there is an SIS department in every unit. There is an assistant commander for SIS in the Split Military District, as well as in the other military districts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you say SIS of the Split Military District -- no. You said SIS, you mean one of the SIS's in Operational Group north, and the one which is part of the HVO which was subordinated at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this becomes Exhibit P1136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1136 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'd also like to tender the next document on this list which is 348 without going into detail, but it is referred to in the report of Mr. Theunens on page 344, and it deals with the same topic. I'd like to tender 65 ter 348, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P1137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1137 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to move on to the next topic. That is enforcement. And in this section I would like to refer to approximately six documents. Enforcement is dealt with by Mr. Theunens in paragraph 66 of his executive summary. This is P1113, and I read just one sentence out of it: "The number of orders the Split Military District Command and its subordinate units issue to prevent arson and looting and the rate at which these orders were released suggests that these orders, as well as the measures by the Split MD commander and his subordinate commanders, to enforce them and verify their implementation lack effectiveness."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's going to the first document, which is 65 ter 4446. And this is a report dated 25th October 1995, titled: Inspection by PD at ZP Split between 17 and 20 October 1995. And it's authored by Major Ante Lausic. And I would like to go to page 3 of this document, and I quote from paragraph 6 on page 3: "While discipline and order are at an appropriate level as regards the level of responsibility for the execution of tasks, they are not at the necessary level in relation to property (military and civilian) and considering the inclination towards incidents (fights, alcoholism, appropriate dress, et cetera). The difficulty of the situation is exacerbated by a complete lack of a functioning civilian authority (in the liberated areas) and elementary infrastructure (utility services, water electricity et cetera). Due to indisciplined conduct of and a lack of sanctions against what has occurred, the theft of property and arbitrary occupation of structures still persists and could cause wider political damage." What is the significance of this comment of lack of sanctions against what has occurred?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as an introduction, on the first page we can see that these are the findings of a member of the political administration at the Ministry of Defence, findings of an inspection he and his team conducted of the Split Military District Command, as well as two subordinate units. To answer the question, what is described by the author by lack of sanction, is a serious situation -- and this is also described in the doctrines of various armies, and it goes from the lowest level command even from the section leader, i.e., an NCO, to the highest level, that if orders and in particular discipline are not enforced and if no measures are taken against behaviour that is not in line with the regulations, then actually that will be seen as an encouragements by the subordinates to repeat the violations. And in that context, I wish to draw your attention to -- if I remember well, it was Article 7 of the 1992 Code of Discipline where the three goals of military discipline were explained, i.e., to correct the perpetrator; secondly to serve as an example; and thirdly, to allow the functioning of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, may I ask you, the report is about inspection 17th to 20th of October. Could you tell us, for example, where it is described here that the civilian -- the lack of a functioning civilian authority, does that cover that period in October, or does it cover a longer period, or is there any clue as far as the specific time-frame of when specifically this paragraph 6 is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document does not allow to draw any conclusions as to which specific time-period the author is addressing. As I mentioned at the beginning of my testimony, I have not analysed the functioning of civilian authorities, expect for the functioning of the Knin garrison command. However, the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District covers a much wider area, so I'm not in a position to draw conclusions on the functioning of civilian authorities in other parts of that zone of responsibility. For what the comments of the author on military discipline are concerned, I have included in my report a series of documents and analysed them that cover the situation prior to, during, and after Operation Storm. And these conclusions that are drawn are in October are coherent with the findings have I in relation to prior events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I do object to the admission of this document on the basis that this is an attachment to a very detailed assessment that was done by the Main Staff. I will be getting into cross-examination on the Main Staff's overall, and it says it is part of an inspection. The inspection was not by the PD, the Political Fairs Branch. It was by the Main Staff. The PD was only one section. I don't know why the Prosecution has taken out one attachment from one service out of an overall global assessment, but it is my intent to tender everything in cross-examination, and I believe that's the more appropriate way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if that would be result in this document finding its way into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... marked for identification and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's marked for identification as a Prosecution Exhibit, and then we'll see whether we still need it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit P1138, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the next document. This is 65 ter 2393. This is tab 49 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an order dated 17 August 1995 by the chief, General Zvonimir Cervenko. And it addresses the following topic, according to the document taking security measures for units returning from the battlefield. And in paragraph 2, it says, and I quote: "Through the chain of command, prevent any unauthorised use of infantry weapon, ammunitions, mines and explosives, and any other form of endangering the lives and properties of the civilian population." And paragraph 3: "The commanders of the military districts and staff units are personally responsible to me for the implementation of these orders -- of this order." Now, I'm specifically interested in the entry on paragraph 2, where it says, "through the chain of command." What's the significance of the chain of command in this respect, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chain of command, Your Honour, means that General Cervenko expects the military district commanders and all other addressees of the order which can be found at the bottom of page 2. I think the English document is a different one on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looks very much like a different document, yes. Which gives me time also to point at page 16, line 6, where the name Lasic is spelled as Lausic, and that could create confusion, although the first name is different from the person with the name of Lausic. Nevertheless, it should be Lasic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I think that is my mispronunciation of the name of Mr. Lasic. Yes, I'm not sure whether we have uploaded the wrong translation in English, and I'll certainly correct the record if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But if you could continue your answer, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Through the chain of command, it means that General Cervenko --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Still we do not have the English on the screen in order to follow the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I -- I have a hard copy which can be put on the ELMO if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's one is looking at the document, the other is to verify whether there is an English translation uploaded into e-court which of course is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... for the mistake, and we'll have it corrected as soon as we can. I also have a copy for the ELMO although it is marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what secrets it reveals, Mr. Waespi, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we go to the second page of the document, at the bottom we see the list of addressees. So it states the commanders of all the military districts. JB, I was not able to establish which organisation that corresponds with, but then the navy, the air force, and the aircraft defence, and this is the copy as we could see on the first page which was received by the forward command post of the Split Military District in Knin. We would have to go to the first page again then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that the Defence could assist us in understanding what JB stands for? If so, we'll hear from you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when General Cervenko, the chief of the Main Staff, refers to the chain of command, he expects that this order be forwarded from the highest level to the lowest level, i.e., that the military district commanders give corresponding instructions to their operational group commanders, the operational group commanders to the brigade commanders and regimen commanders, these commanders to the next echelon, i.e., the battalion level, subsequently, the company level, the platoon level, and then the section level. Why? Because this is it an order that has to be implemented by everybody, and mainly by the individual soldiers, who is as is it explained in the first paragraph, upon their return from the battlefield, we see there is a rotation of units, units which have been participating in Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move it a bit so that we have a better look at the content of -- move it. Yes, even a bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is it everything. Well, I would like to read it before it is take away, if you would not mind. I'd just like to read a couple of lines starting with the: "On the basis of operational reports."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the situation, Mr. President, is that we have rotations of units, units are returning from the combat or the former combat zone and are going to their peacetime barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could get foundation why he thinks they're coming from a former combat zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe the word former is -- what I described to describe is that Operation Storm has officially concluded on the 9th. Of course, there are still skirmishes in the zone that has recently regained control of. There are still search operations for remaining resistance pockets and the like. But we also see, and this happens actually already earlier, on the 9th, as far as the Split Military District is concerned, on the 9th of August, an order is given by General Gotovina to reorganise the Operational Groups. Whereby what is described as the first line units, the professional units, like the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade, are called back. They are sent on leave, even though some elements are kept there reserve. For example, one battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade is kept in reserve in Knin. But the units which are on the first line during Storm are replaced by units which were like in the back during the conduct of Operation Storm, in particular, Home Guard Regiments. And this is a rotation process whereby units return to their peacetime barracks or parts of units. And based operational reports, as General Cervenko describes it, some of these units, those who are left the battlefield, as he calls it, to return to their peacetime locations, have opened infantry fire in populated places and thus, as he described it, endangered the lives and Safet of the population and disturbed public law and order. I know it's not part of my testimony, but when I was in Zagreb with UNPROFOR, we were aware -- and I don't recall which weekend it was, but during one of the weekends, units came back, units from the Zagreb garrison, for example, elements of the 1st and the 2nd Guards Brigade. We had received instructions from the UNPF command to stay inside. We could hear from our locations that during the night of Saturday and Sunday, there was a significant amount of light arms fire which we didn't hear during other nights. And therefore, we made the association of the return of the units, which was covered in the media, and this increased in fires incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were people shooting at the returning units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The returning units as a matter of expressing their joy, used weapons to fire in the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will understand why I asked this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an obvious question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It makes a distinction between conclusion an observation. You heard more than usual small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Normally you didn't hear any small-arms fire in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking whether somebody was shooting at these humans --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So based on the reporting we received and previous knowledge of the conflict, without going into too far details, but for example, the British UNPROFOR troops, they had grid maps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's focus on this document and the question that was put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I respond and tell that you JB means in Croatian Juzno Brijeste which is the southern front, and it refers to the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting us, Mr. Misetic. You were explaining about this order returning -- units returning from the battlefield, and could we also have a look at the second page so we can see what the order is about. Please proceed, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. So now which see the instructions given by General Cervenko to the commanders of the military districts, the commander of the southern front as well as the commander of the navy, the air force, and the anti-aircraft defence. The first instruction is quite logical. That is that all weapons ammunition, mines, and explosive have to be collected before the people can return. And normally you only have ammunition on your weapon when you go into an operation when you return from the operation before, and this applies also to exercises, before people leave the zone of operations or in case of training, the training area, or the -- they have to hand in the ammunition. In this particular case, also weapons in order to avoid all possible, not only accidents among the military members but also as General Cervenko described it earlier in the order, incidents of indecent firing. In the second paragraph, we have the reference to the chain of command, to prevent any unauthorised use of fire infantry weapons, ammunition, mines and explosives or other activities that can endanger the lives and properties of the civilian population. The civilian population here is the civilian population in the peacetime locations of these units, i.e., the locations to which these units return. The last paragraph is -- is an implementation of doctrine. That is that a superior commander, chief of the Main Staff holds his next subordinate commander responsible, personally responsible, for the implementation of the order. In this context it is also important to note that Cervenko, in accordance with the doctrine, and the duties of commanders that he holds the operational commanders responsible for the implementation and the enforcement of military discipline because this is an aspect of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you in relation to 1 and 2, 1 says return of units only if they have -- if all the weapons, ammunition, et cetera, has been collected and warehoused, so no one is in possession of any arms anymore. Two, it says "unauthorised use of infantry weapons." I do understand that nobody has use of infantry weapons anymore. How could you reconcile 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reconcile 1 and 2 by considering that in paragraph 1 reference is primarily made to weapons that have been found during or collected during the operations as a part of war booty. It is true, and we'll see that later when she is records are discussed in my report, that orders given through the chain of command for the collection of war booty but -- it is difficult to prevent except if one has continuous controls and orders that soldiers will try to keep their personal souvenirs or war trophies. And I remember again from when I was in Zagreb in August 1995 that very harmless souvenirs like road indication signs but also more harmful souvenirs were taken from the areas that had been recaptured or the recaptured partings of Croatia to the peacetime locations. So in my view, 1 refers to war booty, and 2 refers to the weapons that are part of the equipment of the soldier, whereby 1 and 2, I want to emphasise that after returning from an operation or from an exercise, ammunition and weapons are separated the in the military, at least the militaries I'm familiar with. They are never transported together. Why? Because of the risk of incidents or accidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mines as war booty is that usual or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if mines are found, and I think we're talking here about mines that have not been planted somewhere or used during operations, but I am familiar with -- again from the documents that I reviewed that the Serb forces, SVK left significant amounts of ammunition and mines and explosives in warehouses. It is important that the military establishes control over these facilities avoids that people who have no right of access -- access these locations and that then this ammunition and mines are transported and stored in accordance with regulations. Now, the fact that General Cervenko includes it in his order, and that he refers to previous reports indicates that there have been incidents whereby mines, explosives, and ammunition and weapons have not been treated in accordance with the regulations and have resulted in -- have been used -- yeah, used in incidents and resulted in injuries among civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you explained to us that it is your interpretation that 1 is mainly concerning war booty, and 2 is their personal -- the weapons that were legitimately in the hands of -- of the units. One talks about military conscripts. Is another interpretation could that would that be 1 is about military conscripts, and 2 is about others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is indeed possible Your Honours. Now, I have -- based on the documents I have seen I have not been able to see whether if conscripts are still in service, whether they are subjected to other regulations or not. Of course, and if the conscripts have been demobilized, the regulations I have seen is that they do not keep weapons let alone ammunition or mines as their personal equipment. It is all handed in. Indeed maybe that is something that I didn't see at first glance now when looking at the monitor, but that is a very important aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the reason why I put this question to you is that you give an explanation, I ask you about how to reconcile 1 and 2, you give an explanation, and as soon as I suggest another explanation, you're quite willing to say that a that is a good explanation as well which, of course, causes me some concern.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the problem that I have been facing from the beginning. Drawing conclusions on single documents, it goes contrary to the methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's why I'm asking you. I'm ask you what the explanation is. I didn't ask you to limit the sources of your explanation to this document. I just asked you how to I have to understand 1 and 2 here. You could have referred to the totality of the documents reviewed, but you give an explanation, and three minutes after that, you -- you would cheerfully share my suggestion of another explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honours, this is an fourth or fifth explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- when I said it is of some concern, how to explain documents when there are four or five possible explanations. I just wanted to share that concern with you. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1139.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we do have an translated uploaded right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P1139 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the next document, which is 65 ter 890.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is an order by commander Colonel Mladen Fuzul dated the 19th August 1995. And it talks about the observed break down of order and discipline and for the international reputation of the Republic of Croatia. And then Colonel Fuzul orders: "1. Establish control in all units and immediately take measures against the torching of buildings and killing of animals. "2. Take disciplinary and criminal measures against irresponsible individuals. "3. The commanders of OG west units are responsible to me for the implementation of this order." Who is Colonel Mladen Fuzul?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see on the top left corner of the document, he is the commander of OG west. Now OG west was formally known as the OG Otric, and during Operation Storm, i.e., between 4th and 9th of August, Colonel Fuzul was the commander of OG Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now we are on the 19th of August, 1995. What is the significance of this order at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction to the transcript. It is Zadar, with a D like Delta, instead of Zapac. The significance of the order is that I have attempted to explain in the report by including earlier documents or earlier reports an orders in relation to the events referred by Fuzul in the introduction of his order. On the 19th of August there are still problems in relation to what he describes as break down of order and discipline. The fact that he issues this order indicates that personnel of his unit, i.e., OG west as well as subordinate units are among those who are responsible for these incidents. If no one from his OG or no one from the military under his command and control was involved in these incidents, there would be no requirement to issue such an order. And the addressees can be seen on the last page of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections Exhibit P1140 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Next document, Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to discuss is 65 ter 2085. And this is a document dated 17 September 1995, and it's signed by Colonel General Ante Gotovina, at least authored. And it reads in the relevant part as follows: "On the basis of the order by the commander of the Split Military District ... dated 17 September 1995, and in order to monitor ever Drvar area by military and police and carry out the tasks from the aforementioned order I hereby order: 1. The commander of the 72nd Battalion of the military police shall immediately transfer one platoon of the military police to Drvar with the task of monitoring access roads to Drvar by military and police and preventing torching and other forms of destruction of property. And 2 talks about the subordination of the military police. And 3, that Colonel Fuzul will be in charge of the work of the military police platoon. Now, first of all, this document obviously concerns incidents in Bosnia. Now why do you include documents in your report that concern incidents in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I include these documents because based on the other material I reviewed for the compilation of this report, I consider these operations a continuation of the -- of Operation Storm whereby these operations are conducted -- this is 17th of September is two days after the ending of operation Maestral. So whereby these operations are conducted by forces operating under the command of Colonel Gotovina, and I consider these documents important not only because they are continuation but because I wanted to see whether again applying the methodology of identifying patterns and trends whether there were any significant differences in relation to what I had observed during Operation Storm and its immediate aftermath.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you discover any significance differences in analysing these documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is one of the conclusions I draw. I emphasise that based on the material I reviewed, I see a difference between the nature of the orders that are issued during and after Operation Storm, with after I mean the immediate aftermath, and orders that are issued during the immediate paragraph math of Operation Maestral, whereby the orders that issued after Maestral are much more forceful. I also, for example, directed -- directly at the military police in order to have them enforce discipline and order and prevent crime, whereby I have not seen such specific and strong orders during Operation Storm, and its immediate aftermath.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now in relation to the subordination of the military police, a topic we discussed last week, what's the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this order is in -- is coherent with the doctrine, Article 9 of the 1994 MP regulations, stating that the military police for regular military police tasks are subordinated to the operational commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P1141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. P1141 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to discuss is 65 ter 709.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is a similar document relating to events in Bosnia. It's an order by General Gotovina dated 22nd September 1995. The subject is establishment of intervention companies to establish order and discipline in the town of Jajace. And specifically it imposes in paragraph 1 a military curfew in the town of Jajace. Again, Mr. Theunens, why did you select this document in your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this order by General Gotovina is -- is coherent with what I described in my previous answer, that is, that during the aftermath of Operation Maestral, we see that General Gotovina issues a number of very strong or forceful orders, in order to maintain order and discipline. Here we have one where he imposes a military curfew in the town of Jajace which is located in Bosnia and Herzegovina and which put on the HV/HVO control during Operation Maestral. I have not seen such a document or an order imposing a military curfew during Operation Storm or the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm. Imposing military curfew is one of the tools the commander has in order to maintain order and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, with respect to foundation, if Mr. Theunens could tell us if he could impose a military curfew in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my conclusion that even though there is information that there was civilian police in the area, i.e., in Croatia whereby I have not seen any information on the presence of civilian police in these parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were put under HV/HVO control, it is my conclusions that the goal, i.e., maintain order and discipline, is the most important aspect. Secondly we have to look who can achieve this goal. We spoke briefly about the aspect of the role of the military in establishing the rule of law. This was not part of my testimony, but I was asked about that. Now when you consider -- when you consult literature on that topic, one notices that immediately after a conflict, and I'm talking now on previous observations I will come to Operation Storm, that in other conflicts the military is usually or only the best organised -- organisation to try to establish rule of law. Why? Because you have the manpower, the organisation, the structure, the system of internal discipline, and last but not least equipment, weapons of all nature. When I look now at Operation Storm, and I want to emphasise that I have not systematically analysed all civilian police documents, but the documents I reviewed and they consist mainly of correspondence between assistant minister Mr. Moric, assistant minister of the interior, as well as General Lausic, chief of the military police administration, the conclusion that I draw is that the civilian police has difficulties in imposing or -- law and order or doing his job in general in the parts of Croatia that been recently recaptured. Moric, Mr. Moric explains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're engaging in a long journey. Mr. Misetic, did you want the witness to explain whether there was any formal authority to impose a military curfew, or were you seeking to hear the background of why --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was not seeking the background, Your Honour, but I will say that - again that is just the position of the Defence - one of the few conclusions that are in the report is this precise point which is the at page 314 paragraph S of Mr. Theunens' report which says: "It appears that only and after launching Operation Maestral, Colonel General Ante Gotovina takes more vigorous action to maintain discipline and prevent or punish crimes." That's his conclusion. I think the witness has now repeated, in essence, that conclusion here. The Prosecution and the witness should establish the foundation in Croatian law, and the witness indicated before that he when challenged on his expertise in law said that any citizen can have a basic understanding of the law, to cite to the law that General Gotovina could impose military curfew on Croatian territory. It shouldn't be a long answer. He should know. It's his conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a legal basis on which you consider General Gotovina in a position of authority to establish military curfew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only base I have, Your Honour, is my interpretation of the Code of Discipline. I have no specific legal base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I speak now. As we are dealing with this document, could the witness please explain as to with regards to count 3 of the order where it says that with the employment of the special police of MUP, Ministry of Interior, does it refer us to the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia or the Ministry of Interior of the republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exceptionally, I allow further questions since they are just seeking an explanation or clarification, rather than a question which would be more appropriately put during your cross-examination. Having heard your answer on the question of what the basis is for the military curfew, could you please address the matter just raised by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Waespi, this is not part of the time you take.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, based on my review of documents and, in particular, documents concerning the operations of the special police of the Republic of Croatia, this reference is to special police of the so-called Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, CRHB and not the special police of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender this document, which is 65 ter 709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1142 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last document in this section, which perhaps we could do before the break, but I'm in your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can deal with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Last document in this series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is 65 ter 851. A document dated the 18th of August 1995, authored by the deputy commander of the Split Military District, Brigadier Rahim Ademi. And it orders the set-up of military police check-points at the Knin-Gracac-Otric cross-roads and has more details about these actions, and in paragraph 5 it makes the commander of the 72nd Battalion of the Split Military District police responsible for the implementation of this order. Now my last question. Again, the significance of these concrete orders in what the military police has to do.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one of the orders that are included in the section of my report dealing with orders issued by the chief of the HV Main Staff or the chief of the -- the commander of the Split Military District, pertaining to the treatment of war booty and goods described as such. Starts on English page 374. Here, this order, specific order, is important because we see the use of the military police upon the orders of the Deputy Commander of the Split Military District to establish a check-point, whereby this check-point can only allow vehicles in that have an appropriate authorisation. We see that in paragraph 3. And according to this order, this check-point is also to prevent the entry of civilian vehicles, which shows, together with the other documents I have reviewed that, at that time, i.e., 18th August, the Split Military District is in a position to exercise control, i.e., to determine who is allowed in and out of its zone of responsibility, and paragraph 4 re-establishes that war booty or goods described as such can only be transported if proper lists signed by the unit commanders are provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you how you conclude from an order that there was sufficient control. It says that a military check-point should be set up. Now, if someone would take the route next to where the military check-point is, what about your conclusion, as far as the control on entering and leaving that area is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The goal obviously of the order is not just to set up a check-point but it is to use that check-point in order to maintain control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's obvious, yes. But now if you say they -- and let me quote you literally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is on page 37, line 2, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "Which shows together with the other documents that I have reviewed at the time the Split Military District is in a position to exercise control."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll tell you why I put this question to you. We have heard quite some evidence where -- of course some witnesses may have come to the same conclusion as you come. Others said, Well, it was very easy to take another route and then you would just circumvent these check-points and then no problem. So the exercise of control, apparently you take this document together with the other document, as you said, as a demonstration that control could be exercised or was even exercised here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For this specific order, Your Honours, one would have to look at the map and see whether there are indeed manners or ways in order to circumvent the military police check-point. However, military police check-points are not the only tool for the military to maintain control. They can also use their forces, for example, to patrol. And even if, like, with most border controls there is no 24/7 waterproof or water-tight regime possible, manning a check-point also includes observing. Now, if for example, the military police notice, well, there's not traffic stopping here, or they see that vehicles are using another road, well, then the chief or the person responsible for the check-point will contact his commander to say, Look, my check-point here is not effective. I propose to locate it somewhere else. The patrols, well, they will report what they see. If people who want to enter the zone of responsibility and who are not authorised to do so notice that there are patrols, check-points -- I mean, here we're talking about a fixed check-point - one can also have mobile check-points - that can serve as a deterrent. I think it is also important to keep in mind that there may still be members of the former enemy forces residing in the area who may try to enter or who may try to disrupt the activities of -- of the forces that are now controlling the area, so the military commander again has all interest in maintaining the strictest control possible. There will always be -- there can always be somebody who can try to get in, but then, well, we will have to look at what vehicle. If it is about looting goods, yeah, I assume that happens with trailers or bigger vehicles. I have seen the area. You cannot just use a trail which may be mined, or a soft-surface road to move heavier vehicles. So I think there is a number of factors the commander will take into account before deciding on putting a check-point in a particular location, and this will be part of a global plan on his side which is aimed at controlling his zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.text: Mr. President I would like to tender the document but only the cover page and Article 27.

utterances.text: Now, Mr. Theunens, based on your review of the documents, the doctrine, how are the police administrations on one side, and the special police on the other side related to each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The last document I want to discuss, it's already an exhibit, is D530. D530. The first one is on the right side, to "SJP commander," and on the left side is to "chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration." And there it adds, "personally deliver to the SJP commander." And the subject is the "Request for verification of information." And the last paragraph: "In keeping with the above, you are to investigates the above claims and submit in writing the results of the investigation to the special police sector." And the issue at hand here are for members of the special police as described in the first substantive paragraph. Now my question, Mr. Theunens, what's the significance of this document in relation to the issue of who commands the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the person who signs -- the name of the persons who signs the document, we can see that Colonel General Mladen Markac is in command of the special police sector. He sends an order to the SJP commander of the of the SUP unit of the Zadar-Knin police administration, through the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, based on the documents I reviewed, in particular those dealing with the role and the use of special police units during and after Operation Storm. The inclusion of the chief of Zadar-Knin police administration is not related to command and control but is an administrative matter. And again the chain of command goes from the assistant minister, to the chief of sector, to the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask one -- you said this is an order that reads subject: Request for verification of information. Could you explain why you consider it an order, rather than a request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in simple terms, when a superior, and in this case it is the highest person within the special police, has a request it is interpreted as an order by the subordinates. In addition, I would like to draw your attention to the last sentence. In the wording of the last paragraph, it sates, "In keeping with the above you are to investigate." For me that is the language one uses in orders. Even if it is called a request, the result or the aim is actually to have the subordinate carry out an activity or undertake an activity. And in this case the activity consists of investigating, I quote, "the above claims." And also the second action the subordinate is required to do following this request is to submit in writing the results of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try to understand also your reasoning behind it. You say in simple terms when a superior and the highest person within the special police has a request is interpreted as order by the subordinates. To what extent are you reasoning in a circle, because you use this document to say that it is sent to a subordinate. To what extent are you reasoning in circles? Because you say the word "request" should be interpreted as an order because that is how it is understood by a subordinate, but at the same time you use this document as evidence that there was subordination. So your interpretation of the document is based on the outcome of your exercise, so some extent, not in every respect, but as far as the interpretation of the word "request" is concerned that is what you apparently told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand what you mean, Mr. President. Now, I didn't use that specific document in my report in the context of command and control because I saw it more important in the context of the disciplinary authority of the command of the special police, i.e., when he receives an information - and I will not go into detail because it drags us too far - he uses powers to request information. But in the first year of Military Academy, we received a brochure for junior officers. And one of things I remember from that brochure is that it stated well, a request by a superior or a wish by a superior should also be -- always be consider add order. Okay. I realize that has no power of law. But that's at least how as a junior person sees or is educated in the military and is trained in order to interpret information, in particular requests or orders he receives from a superior. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But isn't it true that the issue raised here is whether the Zadar-Knin police administration is subordinated to Mr. Markac. That's the issue, isn't it? At least you -- that's what you understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The issue is -- this document shows together with other documents that the special police unit of the Zadar-Knin police administration is subordinated to Markac, General Markac. It is it not the Zadar-Knin police administration as such because that is the regular police which follows a different chain. We are talking about the SJP unit. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And because you say personally delivered to SJP commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says both, isn't it? Now the handwriting comes from whom? Because it's in the handwriting -- no, let me just try to see in the original. No, you say I should focus on the SJP commander more than the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry that I cannot explain why the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration is included here. utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.
