utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to explore with you an issue that we talked about briefly last week that you addressed on page 180 and 181 of your report, and that would be part 2 of your report, concerning the shelling conducted by the Split Military District during Operation Storm. The focus of this will begin on paragraph 9(A), the last sentence 9(A)(i) where you write: "Duties of the Split Military District artillery include: 'Putting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire without indicating any specific targets in Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, the Split Military District artillery is to engage.'" You carried that yet further on the next paragraph: "The fact that the orders of subordinate units, the operative group Zadar, orders for artillery dated 3 August 1995 instructs that you put the following towns under artillery fire Benkovac, Obrovac, Gracac that were reviewed during the preparation of this report do not contain more specific targeting information, either suggests that the Split Military District commander and its subordinate commanders regard these Serb controlled towns as military targets that can be engaged with artillery." And on the next page you support this conclusion with an order from Brigadier Ademi dated 7th of May, 1995. And I would like to explore that conclusion that you've made. But preliminary I'd like to ask you, when you were given instructions -- by the way let me just backtrack for a second, just to put this in sequence. When was the first time you received instructions from a member of the Office of the Prosecutor as to what they wanted you to do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- if I remember well, it was in January 2007. We had -- I apologise for the transcript. In December we had this first inform meeting where I spoke about my experience. So December 2006, where I spoke about my experiences in the UNPROFOR UNPA headquarters, and then in January 2007, I believe at the end of the month, I received the ten-point tasking which has been addressed at the beginning of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At that time, were you given instructions or were you told by the Office of the Prosecutor that the Office of the Prosecutor would argue in this trial that Knin and other towns in the Krajina were indiscriminately attacked with artillery by the HV?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was not given any instructions whatsoever in relation to what I was to write in my report. I only received the ten-point and subsequently the 17-point list which basically dealt with or covered the topics I was to deal with. I did not receive any instructions or guidance whatsoever in relation to the contents of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay sir. Let's maybe put a little bit of a finer point on this without taking it too far. When did you first learn that the Office of the Prosecutor was going to argue that Knin and these other towns in Krajina were indiscriminately fired upon with artillery? When did you first learn that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Maybe it is included in the indictment. I read the indictment once, in the beginning of this whole project to find out the time-frame and the geographic areas I was to cover. I am aware and I heard that from Dai Morris that there is it going to be an artillery expert, but that is how far my knowledge on this issue goes. And if you allow me, I don't claim that the shelling was indiscriminate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not the question you have been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk about this entire matter a bit further and go through the methodology, if you will, and look at some of the issues that you looked at. And I note on page 81 and 82 of your report -- and again if I don't mention it, Mr. Theunens, I'm talking about part 2 of the report. I think that's for clarity's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps I started talking when the witness had not yet finished his answer, and this has caused some loss in the transcript. I think the witness started explaining that it was not his position that there was indiscriminate shelling, and then I intervened and said that as far as I was aware that was not the question you had put to him. That was missing on the transcript due to me not waiting, and I would like to correct that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to what -- your report itself. And I am informed that this at page 339 in e-court. You note at the bottom of the page that the HV Main Staff in June, July issues several directives an orders to Military Districts including the Split Military District, to launch and conduct operation called Oluja, taking into account the launching of Operation Ljeto, or Summer 95 on 25 July 1995. "It can be included that these directives and orders are amended over time and implemented in a modified form." Let us start that, and let's just explain that just a bit further, Mr. Theunens, with regard to the implementation of these orders that commenced Operation Storm. And I'm most interested in your comment that these directives an orders are amended over time and implemented in a modified form. Can you help us with that a little bit and just explain that a bit.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was reviewing the material, I came across orders from the HV Main Staff which mentioned the name Oluja, which as those quoted in the pages listed by Mr. Kehoe, date, for example, from the 26th of June. When you review the contents of these orders, one will note that some of the instructions included in these orders were actually already achieved or implemented during operation Ljeto. And that's why -- I mean, I still included them as background, but in my view, the authorative order for Operation Storm, on the level of the Split Military District, is the order for attack Kozjak which used to be 65 ter 3119, has been tendered. I don't have the exhibit number, which can be found on English page 96.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will get to those, Mr. Theunens, in a little bit. But what you were trying to convey during this type when orders were coming out from the Main Staff and going down to the middle -- Military District, there was a constant exchange of information both up and down from the General Gotovina Military District Commander level that caused these plans to change, given new intelligence coming in, new information coming in, you mentioned changes in the terrain after summer 1995. All of those elements come into play for a military commander to constantly monitor, and orders change. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is accurate and that is what called the command process in part 1 of my report. And again, it relates to situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just take this and go through with the Chamber with the assistance of your report because some of the reports are in different places, and I would like to go through a sequence with you. And I will tell you, Mr. Theunens, I believe that absent one or two which I will identify for you all of the documents that we will go through have been set forth in footnotes of your report. You can question me if I am incorrect, but I believe I have done that to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to 65 ter 4481.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is, in fact, a document that you discuss on page 82 of your report or page 340 in e-court. I will talk episodically about some other issues here, but I want to focus mostly on the artillery issues. And this is an order that came from General Bobetko on the 26th June 1995. And for all intents and purposes, Mr. Theunens, this is the first directive focussed on Storm. Although it had been discussed in other capacities, this is the first one; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first one I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As early on in this report, if we could turn to page 6 of 11 in this report. Before we get to it, what is this? What is this directive? Just explain it to the Chamber generally.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the hierarchy of orders and commands, if I can express myself in that way, as I have addressed in part 1 of the report directives is the second highest level. The highest level are instructions. Then you have directives, and subsequently, you go down until you have, at the end commands which are the most simple forms of orders, so a directive is an order from -- which is issued by the highest military level, i.e., the Main Staff, and it contains detailed information and instructions as to the tasks of the units of the HV. In this context this is a directive which includes tasks for the Split Military District, in relation to the conduct of an operation identified as Storm or Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 6 of this document, and we will go through the whole document because we will put it into evidence for review by the Chamber. But I'm interested in on page 6 of 11, paragraph 7, the artillery and rocket support. It notes that artillery and rocket support will be provided by the 14th and 20th. And then next paragraph: "The support should focus on neutralizing the Republika Srpska Main Staff and the 7th corps command post in Knin, the brigade command posts, concentrations of enemy manpower, armour and artillery in the area of Knin and Benkovac, including ammunition depots, while supporting the main forces in attack and preventing an enemy counterattack from the direction of Knin, Kastel Zegarski, and Benkovac." And if we could just turn to page 9, I just want to ask you a couple of questions on this artillery issue. In the middle of the page: "On the basis of the newly collected information ..." Do you see that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, Mr. Kehoe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "On the basis of the newly collected information about changes on the enemy's side, you are to update the plans of operation, particularly the plans for the use of artillery and HRZ as well as the other plans, all of which are to be submitted to the Main Staff -- the HV Main Staff." When you reviewed this you concluded, did you not, that very early on that the HV Main Staff had specific military targets in mind in planning Oluja and that those plans were to be updated with additional information concerning the use of artillery as time went on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. But at the beginning of the order, we also see that the order is based on the plans that have been proposed by the commander of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But this is a specific idea that the Main Staff has on military targets and that is to be updated, especially the use of artillery, has to be updated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how command and control is implemented. It is then up to the commander of the Split Military District in this case to determine the specific targeting information and provide that specific information to his artillery units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 4481.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that becomes Exhibit D956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D956 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the order that we just viewed is just a small example of the complexities that are involved in conducting a military operation, like Oluja or any such operation. Would you agree with that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we turn your attention to -- well, in addition to the order that came down from General Bobetko on the directive, there is an specific order that General Bobetko sends to General Gotovina on the 26th June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could bring up 65 ter 1283.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the first order -- the first directive that we just talked about previously is a directive being sent to one person specifically. This document appears just to be send to General Gotovina. Can you help the Chamber out just a bit as to the distinction between these two, Mr. Theunens? If you want to review the document, we can scroll through it but ...

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is logical that orders, or actually all correspondence from the superior commander is send to the -- to the commander of the subordinate unit -- no, I will rephrase that. I apologise. If a superior wants to send information or requests something from a subordinate unit, he will send his request or his order to the commander of that unit, so it is logical that an instruction or an order for the Split Military District from the HV Main Staff is sent to the commander of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's -- in fairness, let's just look through the document. It will be a little easier to have you answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could I seek some clarification in relation to this directive. I think your first questions were about specific towns or villages, and what you just read to the witness in this artillery and rocket support, 7, deals with Knin only. Whereas elsewhere in the document I think I read something about artillery access. Now what I like to clarify with the witness is you said, is it true that from this directive we learned that they had specific targets. To what extent is that true for the whole of the operation or for Knin or for -- in view of your conclusions, I'm trying to understand exactly what we can learn from this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, you wish me to comment on the previous document we saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The previous document. You were asked questions. Mr. Kehoe asked you whether you would agree whether there were specific targets, and I think in relation to 17 that they had to be updated. And you were taken from one portion was about Knin and to a more general portion about updating of targets. What I'd like it know is -- let me just see what Mr. Kehoe exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would be helpful if we flipped back to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or the line exactly where you put it. You were asked by Mr. Kehoe, "Once you had been taken to the targets, which as far as I understood were limited to Knin, you were asked when you reviewed you concluded that that very early on that the HV Main Staff had specific military targets in mind in planning Oluja and that those plans were to be updated with additional information concerning the use of artillery as time went on? " That was question was put to you after you had been taken to the artillery support, which was about targets in Knin, and when you had been taken to this paragraph which said, Well, we have to update on the basis of new information. Now the conclusion that was put to you by Mr. Kehoe was not in any way limited to Knin but was rather general in nature. When you said, "that's correct," and then you said something about the plans were proposed by the Split Military District commander, did you mean to agree with Mr. Kehoe that this was in general the case; or did you agree with Mr. Kehoe on the basis of what he had put to you, that is, about Knin, and if I could say so, the update paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my answer applied to the general situation. That is that in the directive from the Main Staff, specific targets as to the nature of the targets. The directive talks about command posts, concentrations of enemy manpower, or concentrations of armour and artillery in the area of Knin and Benkovac, including ammunition and fuel depots, so in the directive of the HV Main Staff, these are the types of targets that are identified. Obviously the Main Staff does not -- or General Bobetko does not state where the targets are exactly located in Knin and Benkovac. Then it is up to the subordinate commander based on the intelligence and information he has to use this guidance or this instruction actually from his superior to determine well, which of these targets -- first of all, where are these targets located which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. My question was mainly focussed on whether you agreed this to be the general approach or whether it was limited to the areas which were specifically put to you by Mr. Kehoe, and I do that you take that this was a general statement about the approach taken at the time. If that is the case, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is indeed the general approach. I think we both -- we all observed that there is an distinction between what is stated in 4481 and what is stated in the order for attack, because there we just see well, just take the city of Knin, Benkovac, and other towns and fire or engage artillery fire against these towns, whereas an earlier instruction from the higher echelon is much more specific. That is the only observation I can make when I compare these two documents. Just to conclude it is illogical that the instruction from the lower level appears to more general and more vague or less specific than the instruction that is coming from the higher echelon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So just taking your last answer, your contention is that the information coming from a higher level is more specific than the information at a lower level, and that's where you find, as you know, that it is illogical for it to be way. Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to say the opposite, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is that the higher echelon, the Main Staff gives the general information. For example, in this specific case, determines the types of targets that are to be engaged, whereas the lower echelon, in this case the Split Military District, will then identify each and every target, and I have included examples of targeting lists in this my report. We discussed that earlier with the X, Y, Z coordinates, the physical identification or name of the target, and so on and so on. This is not for the Main Staff. This is for the Military District and its subordinate units to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Mr. Theunens. Let us go back to the document on the screen, 65 ter 1283, the order from General Bobetko. I believe it is of the same date, or the 26th of June. And this order notes several informational items to bring to General Gotovina's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could scroll up on that first paragraph. "In the last month the enemy has carried out a number of operations that have result in the significant changes in the military and political situation in the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia. This refers mainly to the recruitment into and reinforcement of the forces of the 39th Banija, 21st Kordun, 15th Lika, and the 7th Knin Corps of the SVK of the army of the Serbian Krajina. "The recruitment is being done with the materiel help of the Yugoslav Army and through a mobilisation of the conscripts in the territory of the FRY." Can you explain that a little bit in the sense of is, in fact, the ARSK building up their forces with the assistance of the Yugoslav Army at the time of this order.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have not specifically analysed the activities of the SVK during that time-period. I am familiar with the fact that early June General Mrksic is sent from Belgrade to take over command of the SVK, and I'm also familiar with the parade on the Slunj training ground which took place on the 28th of June 1995. I cannot draw further conclusions as to whether or not the SVK was stepping up its combat readiness or taking other measures. I do remember information from when I was working the UNPROFOR headquarters that there were a lot of expectations from the arrival of Mrksic as to the improvement of the overall capabilities of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we go into this just a bit further, you noted on page 69, line 8, "that I have not specifically analysed the activities of the SVK during that time-period." In P1011, on point ten, point 9, you were instructed that -- by Mr. Tieger in the categories that were to provide information on the pace and progress of Operation Storm, including mop-up operations SVK deployment and activity. So you -- according to the instructions that you received and the exhibit introduced into evidence by the Prosecution, you were given instructions concerning, provide information on SVK deployment and activity. Are you now saying that you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific wording of point 9, but I believe it refers to the situation after Storm when we talk about mop-up operations. I'm not sure -- I don't remember being tasked with a systematic analysis or a detailed analysis of SVK activities prior to Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's pull it up, so maybe we talk -- bring up P1011, page 2, point 9, maybe you can point us out on this. If you can read with me point 9 which is part of your categories to provide information. "Pace and progress of Operation Storm, including mop-up operations; SVK deployment and activity."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding -- and again as you see I have not specifically addressed it in my report. I never -- I didn't hear any comments of the Prosecution in relation to that, but my understanding here is that it actually refers to SVK deployment and activity during and after Operation Storm, and there I can frankly answer that I didn't have access to specific information as to that -- as to the SVK deployment and activity during and after Operation Storm in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that while you were providing this -- I think it's described as a road map for the Chamber, you did not analyse SVK documents concerning deployment and activity during Storm, and thereafter. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I came across such documents but -- no, I will rephrase. I came across a few documents indicating there was actually there was not so much - at least in former Sector South - there was not so much anymore of a SVK deployment and activity -- I mean there was isolated activities. That's again based on the information I remember from working UNPROFOR, but I have not come across documents here indicating that in the course of Operation Storm there was still a functioning command and control and reporting system, the SVK would that provide sufficient documents and reports and orders allowing me to analyse the activities of the SVK in Sector South during that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, is it your testimony that in the OTP archive there were no -- I don't want to overstate the point, sir - there was an insufficient number of SVK documents in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor to allow to you review matters before, during and after; or are you just saying that you didn't review any of those?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key words are "during and after Operation Storm." What happened before I have addressed in very general terms in the report because I thought it was important as background. I have also spoken about, for example, what I'm trying to is a say is that during and after there were not sufficient documents, i.e., documents covering SVK activities in Sector South during and after Operation Storm. I have come across VJ documents covering these issues, but that was long after the filing of the addendum in the framework of the compilation of the an addendum from former Martic report for the Perisic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, when you were putting your documents together, and you received this instruction for whatever it means, did you ask the OTP for any further SVK documentation? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I did not ask the OTP for additional SVK documentation because I didn't consider it of such a high relevance for my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you were providing -- got instructions to provide the Chamber with a road map of what was happening in Operation Storm, you made a decision not to consider SVK documents because you didn't think they were of a high relevance to your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that is what I'm saying. What I'm saying is that I came across documents, including SVK documents, but in relation to the SVK documents not in sufficient number that would allow me to provide a picture that corresponds with the methodology I apply for the operations conducted by SVK the during and after Operation Storm. I remember - and that is not addressed in my report - that the units of the SVK in Sector South quite soon -- at a quite early stage started to withdraw. I also remember that for Sector North there is a cease-fire agreement which is concluded by General Stipetic, Petar, and I'm not sure whether it was Bulat [phoen], or another SVK General on the 8th or 9th of August which resulted in the withdrawal of what remained of (organised SVK units from Sector North). The ten-point list I received from the Prosecution, it was not stated to me that this was a road map for the Trial Chamber. It was followed by 17-point list, then by my proposal of a table of contents. And this proposal which did not cover SVK during and after Operation Storm was accepted by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just flip back to page 1 of this document, just for clarity sake, Mr. Theunens, so you and I are speaking on the same page here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if your point is that the witness, despite the instructions in point 9, did not pay specific attention to the SVK, then that point is made approximately four to five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I show him one sentence. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll drop it, Judge. I think we can go back into the direction we were going. I don't know if Your Honour wants to have a break at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was thinking about that. We'll have a break until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. If we can just go back to 65 ter 1283, please. And if we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we note at the bottom of this paragraph, it notes the issue that the VRS, the army of the Republika Srpska, and the SVK army of the Serb Krajina will carry out an operation to crush the 5th corps of the army of Bosnian and Herzegovina in western Bosnia. That is referring to the Bihac enclave where 5 corps was; is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I would just like to emphasise that this is the intelligence, the SV Main Staff has. So contrary to their intelligence, those are the intentions of the SVK and the VRS in relation to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That, in fact, did happen that the SVK and the VRS engaged in a joint operation at Bihac, did they not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, not at that time. They had done at earlier occasions but the operations from early July only included forces of the SVK together with elements of the forces of the so-called autonomous province of western Bosnia. And I remember that because together with my chief in the G2 in the military office in Zagreb, we had to give a briefing to go Mr. Akashi, and we considered the involvement of the -- of the VRS a key indicator as to the intentions of the SVK and the APWB forces in relation to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you have a tendency to explain a lot even matters which are not specifically asked, because Mr. Kehoe wanted to know whether it did happen, and apart from your answer is that you explain why you remember. If there's any doubt as to your recollection, Mr. Kehoe certainly will address the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, just turning to the next page, if we go into the order itself from General Bobetko, which I'm sure that you are familiar with. That puts the 4th Guards Brigade and the 7th Guards Brigade in readiness. I believe it's at the bottom of the B/C/S version on page 2 and the English version. And if we can go to the next page. It notes in paragraph 6 that the troops -- have the troops ready to carry out their task at by 29 June 1995, 0500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer 65 ter 1283 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit number D957 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is just one further question or two on this document. This document informs General Gotovina of a potential offensive with -- against 5 corps in western Bosnia as well as information concerning the recruitment of additional soldiers. And would you agree that this was information that important because the Split Military District commander or any military commander has to know what he is facing; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He has to know what he is facing, and he has to know his own forces in situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in that situational awareness, he makes decisions based on the information he has on the other side?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He makes a decision based on all the information he has, and the activities of the enemy or the assessed activities of the enemy is only one element of information a commander is considering in order to implement command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when you were going through your methodology and trying to make a decision whether General Gotovina was operating as a reasonable military commander under the circumstances, how did you make that decision when you didn't know what General Gotovina was facing at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not been requested to conclude whether or not General Gotovina was operating as a reasonable military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So -- that's fine, sir. The Defence will accept that answer. Let us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just so can we be clear, so, Mr. Theunens, based on the work that you did, you have no opinion as to whether or not General Gotovina was operating as a reasonable military commander during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have drawn conclusions which can be found in the executive summary. Now, obviously some of these conclusions are relevant or may be relevant for the question whether or not General Gotovina acted as a reasonable military commander, but my -- for my own concern, I was not requested to formulate a specific conclusion as to whether or not General Gotovina acted as a reasonable military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, can you help us, sir, based on your answer, where you say: "I have drawn conclusions which can be found in the executive summary." Now obviously some of these conclusions are relevant or may be relevant for the question of whether or not General Gotovina acted as a reasonable military commander." Now on those issues where that becomes relevant, my question remains for you how could you come to those conclusions in any fashion without knowing what General Gotovina was facing on the other side?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like you to explain what you mean by without knowing what General Gotovina was facing on the other side, and, secondly, as I explained before - and it can also can be found in part 1 of the report - enemy situation is only one aspect a commander has to consider in order to implement the command and control process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I think so we can be clear, I think you know full well that I'm talking about the enemy forces that General Gotovina was facing, be the SVK or the VRS or any other force. I think you know that is what I'm talking about. My question goes back to any conclusion that you could possibly make, how could you make that or make a determination whether or not General Gotovina operated as a reasonable military commander without the assessment, an assessment, as to what he was facing and what he was facing against enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the conclusions I draw in the executive summary is that there is prior to, during, and paragraph Operation Storm a functioning command and control system in the Split Military District that also applies to other forces that operate under the command of General Gotovina during that time-period. I believe that from the military point of view, that is a very important conclusion. And such a conclusion does not have to rely on any information whatsoever in relation to enemy activity, yes or no, because it only refers to the activities of the forces under the command of General Gotovina. If you want, I can give other examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me that when making a decision on whether artillery was used properly or improperly, by a reasonable military commander, it is important for you to assess what that reasonable military commander was facing when a decision was made to use artillery. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have included in my report at different locations in part 2 documents indicating that the Split Military District, through the intelligence it received from the HV Main Staff, as well as from its own intelligence organs, i.e., those at the Split Military District Command level, including, for example, unmanned aerial vehicles which were quite sophisticated for that time, as well as the intelligence organs of its subordinate units. I have concluded from these documents that the Split Military District immediately prior to Operation Storm has updated information as to the location of enemy units, facility, command posts as well as the intentions and activities of these enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, then, taking that one step further, you would agree that General Gotovina based on that information operated as a reasonable military commander because he had specific targeting information to use artillery against, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the tasking I received and the documents I was able to review do not allow to conclude what General Gotovina and his -- and the members of the Split Military District commander operating under his orders did with that intelligence. I can only conclude that they have the intelligence. I have some entries, but I would consider them rather sketchy of subordinate units indicating, for example, as I mentioned on English page 187 that indeed there exists target lists, which I established in accordance with the doctrine I am familiar with. I have an entry that's on English page 188 this is from a report compiled by the 134Th home regiment -- Home Guard Regiment which is 65 ter 4600, and I quote: "Corrections by the means of artillery were done in good time. In the first few hours, we had no support from the Zadar operation group, except for shelling of the area of Benkovac without monitoring. And the message at 0530 hours of the following contents is anything falling on Benkovac." Now I did not draw any overall conclusion for the use of artillery by the Split Military District from that information because I had, in my view, not sufficient information available as to the implementation of the use of artillery firing during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that I can -- given this concession, I think I can cut this -- not concession, but statement. I think I can cut through it a little more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just try to understand what exactly happened over the last two minutes. You asked several times, totally valid question whether you would need knowledge of what the opposite party would do in order to -- to act as a reasonable commander. The witness thought about it a while, and finally instead of directly answering your question, he started explaining to us that in the report, we find elements where apparently, at least, the witness concludes that there was information, perhaps not everything but at least he gave examples of that. And then you said, To therefore you agree that he acted as a reasonable commander. The problem in the line of questioning - and I just want you to know at least what was on my mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that simplified it says, Do you need information to act as a reasonable commander? Let's just assume the answer is yes. Second, did he have information. He had some information. Third, therefore you agree that he acted as a reasonable commander. Which, of course, totally depends. Even if you need information, it doesn't mean that if you have that information that by that reason alone, you act as a reasonable commander. You can act totally unreasonable with that information. It took the witness a while to struggle himself through that. But that is, as a matter of fact, what you strongly suggested in your questions. And whatever the witness would have said, the logic which you presented to the witness is - unlike your first question - is not valid logic. I just want you to be aware of if you -- if you more or less use logical thoughts, then of course the Chamber will apply its own valid logic on these matters. To that extent, I think the factual information that might have assisted the Chamber could have elicited rather quickly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I took that exercise in an attempt to make a curtail of this a bit. I will try to get through it as quickly as possible. If I can turn to 65 ter 3054, and this a order from General Bobetko dated 27 June 1995. If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, it notes in the second-to-last line: "You are to start preparing and making combat documentation as per enclosure number 5 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can scroll it over so they can see the number a bit. You can see it says enclosure, but there's a number 5 there. If we can go to page 4 of 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a list of documents that are prepared for this offensive. Obviously the order of attack, the decision to attack with maps 1:100.000. And it numbers any number of items up to 31. And the -- number 7 is the plan of artillery operation on a map with textual and tabular presentation. What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be like it is explained on the document because I don't see the annex in front me. I would expect that there will be tables indicating the targets, and identifying them. And the map will be used as supportive element.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 2411.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 65 ter 3054.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes Exhibit D958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D958 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your review of the documentation, you did note that General Gotovina did go through the exercise of preparing information in accordance with this order by General Bobetko; did he not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me on which page of my report I discussed this order? Because I'm not sure whether I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You talk about it in - let me see --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were talking about something on the 27th, and this is the 19th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe it is page 84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part 1 or part 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what 84 is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have it now. I could not conclude from this document what actions that General Gotovina undertook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us stay with this document and just go into things like maps. And let's give the Chamber an idea of what we're talking about here and what type of maps are -- the Main Staff expects to be prepared. And let just look at 65 ter 5039. We will look through a series of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is map 14 in the Court binder, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now without going into this document specifically, these are the types -- this is the type of map that is prepared, is it not, when you are going through a planning operation to make a decision how to conduct an offensive. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the best example, Your Honours, because this is actually a summarizing map which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. It is a summary, but what I'm getting at is this the type of planning map that is done at the Split Military District level that is sent up to the Main Staff, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to doctrine it should be -- maps are prepared at all command levels in order to visualize the order and, yeah, it can be sent upwards. But I have no knowledge what this maps actually means. I believe it means that it shows the progress of the units of the Split Military District during Operation Storm. In addition I'm not familiar with the maps that were produced by the Split Military District Command as a result of the order or the directive of General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to cut this short. Is there any dispute about preparing such an operation by the use of maps on which you set out what your plans are? If that is issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... just the visual, Judge, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll just offer into evidence this 65 ter 5039, as a similar map 65 ter 5047, and a last map for Kozjak prepared by Brigadier Ademi, D63005.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection. I would like to see them of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are just introduced into evidence for the purpose of establishing that maps were used for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Might perhaps even have accepted it without looking at them, but since there are no objections, at least not for the time being. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put them -- in view of the common purpose, we put them under one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have noted one correction. On the last map it is 1D630052. My apologies, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these three maps become Exhibit number D959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D959 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note at page 89 in part 2 of your report that there was a meeting in Brijuni that President Tudjman called, and this is a transcript, P461 - no need to bring it up - where were the president says: "Gentlemen I have called this meeting to assess the current situation to hear your views before I decide what our next steps should be in the forthcoming days." I would like to play a short clip for you, and the clip itself from the tape is 1D63-0001.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "President: Is an attack on Knin possible without hitting the camp, anyone UNCRO over there, UNPROFOR ... "Ante Gotovina: At this moment we can engage in extremely precise operations in Knin in a planned manner without aiming at the barracks in which UNCRO is located. "Davor Domazet: Mr. President, we have all the photographs. It is precisely known where who is ... UNPROFOR in the southern barracks, in those southern barracks, and all of their forces are north. Therefore we can fire very precisely without hitting the UNPROFOR camp. It is separate. A bit south of Knin, it is possible to attack precisely. "Ante Gotovina: At this moment none of our weapons operate without guidance, meaning, direct guidance."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will note for you, Mr. Theunens, that in your report you note that at this moment we can engage in extremely precise operations in Knin systematically, whereas this translation is in a planned manner. Now let us take this, sir, when you read this, and you noted General Gotovina talking about the attack on Knin being an extremely precise manner what did you understand -- what did you believe as an intelligence analyst him to mean?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the targets -- I mean for what artillery is concerned that the targets you intend to engage are also the targets that are engaged and that any dispersion of fire is purely within the technical limits of the weapon and that no untended targets are hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did you understand General Gotovina when using the words "extremely precise," that he was -- as an intelligence analysis, did you conclude that he was discussing extremely precise targets?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it is the nuance in English, but I would say extremely precise targeting, i.e., the act of engaging a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now there is also a notation that he notes that we have photographs. Now when you saw that, sir, what did you conclude that General Gotovina -- as an intelligence analyst, what did you conclude General Gotovina was talking about when he said, We have photographs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned earlier, I link that to the entry in General Gotovina's book where he talks the availability of imagery collected from UAVs, unmanned aerial vehicles, and I concluded from that that it would allow him to have access to very precise information as to the locations of targets and the identification of targets as long as these photos are up-to-date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we noted that he says extremely precise operations with photographs. And the translation as we've presented to you says, "in a planned manner." And I must tell you that is different that what is in your report which uses the word "systematically." Now I understand that you are not a B/C/S linguist, sir, but if the translation is, "in a planned manner with precise locations and photographs," as an analyst would you conclude that General Gotovina is telling President Tudjman that we have photographs; we a precise targets in mind; we have a plan to operate in an organised way and in a very planned manner. Would that, as an intelligence analyst, be your assessment from this tape?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I answered the question. I discussed this actually on page 182, English page 182 of part 2 of the report, where I included an excerpt of the minutes of this meeting during which General Gotovina addresses actually the capabilities of his forces in relation to Knin. And that can be found on English page 10 of P461. And systematically, did not change anything -- I mean the word "systematically," to my understanding because I understood it as if you can do it in a manner that -- that is planned and organised, i.e., there is an system behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now -- Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D63-001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'd first like to see the tape. That obviously relates to a tape that we have in evidence, and we just need to compare the two versions. So I'd like to reserve my final judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, on the basis of a balance of probabilities, may I take it that's fair chance that it is not something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, and I didn't give you a time-limit for the maps earlier which you wanted to look at, you have 24 hours to look at the maps. You also have 24 hours to check whether this material is what you expect it to be, and we already decide on admission. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D960 is admitted into evidence, with the proviso I just gave. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I just want to cover one area quickly before we end the day, and I believe it has to do with the intelligence-gathering compatibilities and work that was done by the HV. I do believe during the course of this morning or possibly this afternoon's discussions you talked about the intelligence capabilities -- or the intelligence gathering by the HV and said information -- it was in fact done. And so for a reference point, if you can, if I may, you in fact talk about this on page 87 and 88 of your report. Again, that is part 2 of the report. My apologies that I don't have the e-court number but -- so you could follow with me. But I think we can move through documents on the intelligence-gathering quite quickly. And if we can start with -- again, these are documents absent one I might talk to you about that are in your report, the first being on 65 ter 609 that you referred to on page 88, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can bring that up. And it's an intelligence report of 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just scrolling down a little bit, that first paragraph has to do with conscripts or -- conscripts in and around Benkovac, talking about 2.250 conscripts. And in the last sentence in that paragraph, it says: "... majority of the forces are grouped in Benkovac ..." Information such as this, and I don't want to be specific and put too fine a point on this, Mr. Theunens, but this is information that a commander at General Gotovina's level would want to know, i.e., where the ARSK is not only gathering their troops but possibly positions those troops might take.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to add that this is a report from a source, i.e., it's a HUMINT report, and as a commander, I would like for corroborative information and, for example, use my other intelligence assets in order to seek confirmation of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just taking what you just said, I mean, you would get this piece of information from a source and then you would go back and see whether or not it was correct.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the next page of this document, it's a piece of information coming from someone from UNCRO, which is kind of interesting. You see: "According to the statement of UNCRO." "The positions of SA 6 rocket systems. Now SA rocket systems are mobile rocket systems, surface-to-air rockets, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. And even without being an air defence expert, they were quite old already by the mid-1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But as a commander, sir, be they old or -- you as a commander would want to know where they were, such as in the last insert here being in Knin?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And I would like to obtain more precise information as to the exact location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the issue? The issue apparently is that the -- in preparing for Operation Storm that you would need information and there would be a wish to obtain such information, and that there was the capacity and ability to obtain such information. Now my question is: Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not from our side, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, I'm listening to all of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just wanted to -- I have a series of documents, if I could just get through them quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But there is -- if there's no dispute about the matter, Mr. Kehoe, why -- I mean, first of all, apart from how logical that is, why spend time on matters which are not in dispute? And I hear -- and I formulated in a rather general way, so, therefore, if that is not in dispute, let's move on to matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In some of the documents here concerning the methodology that was employed, there is a dispute, not that they were gathering information, but the specificity information, because it then follows down from, for instance, the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Then focus your question on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do not then ask the witness whether would one would wish to have this information; but if it is the specificity of the information, ask him about that. Because if that is in dispute, then the Chamber, of course, would like to hear what the witness can tell us about a matter which is in dispute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can turn to 1D63-0002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I will tell you that I do not believe, Mr. Theunens, that this is a document that was in your report. Mr. Theunens, this is again an intelligence report from 17 July, and it notes it's information received from the civilian police who are in contact with UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just give the witness a little better view of that, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And tell me, Mr. Theunens, when you're satisfied, we'll go to the next page, if we can.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is in fact the issue that -- as it comes to, targeting that I would like to discuss with you. We see in the first paragraph the intelligence information talks about radar systems. As we move down the page, concentration of troops. And further down the page, there's a presence of tanks and then some mortar batteries. And in each one of those there are the coordinates, the X/Y coordinates, where it shows the locations as to where they are. Now, on those locations -- are you with me, sir?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On those locations, that's the type of information someone that is engaged in picking targets for an artillery attack want [sic]. Isn't that right? The actual coordinates, so you can be a little bit more -- you can be as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And the information has to be timely. And in this case, again, it seems to HUMINT report. For the air defence systems, well, when they are active, they will send out electronic signals. And I assume that the Split Military District has electronical intelligence assets which allow, based on these electronic signals, to exactly determine where this weapon system is deployed and whether it's active. So you will not just rely on a HUMINT report, but you will collect from different sources as much information as possible in order to have the best, precise information in a timely fashion and up-to-date, available at the time you need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D63-0002.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D961, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D961 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I give you the same instructions that I gave you before; that is, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, irrespective of whether it has been given already or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. Yes, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I have a slight practical question. I understood initially that my testimony was to last until 28 of November, and I accepted an invitation from University of Amsterdam to give a lecture on the 3rd of December in the afternoon. I have checked the court schedule for December, and I understand that this Trial Chamber sits in the afternoon that week. Now, maybe my testimony has been -- has concluded by that time, but it would be helpful to me if I could inform the people at the university in Amsterdam as soon as possible about my availability, whether I have to be here or whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your lecture would be in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there are two issues. The first one whether it should necessarily be in the afternoon or whether it can be moved; I don't know whether there's any way of changing that. And second is whether you have already then by then finished your testimony. Well, the last question is rather difficult to answer for me. But the parties have also heard your question. They'll certainly inform the Chamber about the timing they have on their mind, but to be quite frank to you, I don't know whether I expect information which makes me very optimistic. We'll consider the matter and -- Mr. Theunens, and we'll see what Amsterdam can expect. We adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, 25th of November, 9.00, Courtroom I.
